content:
Introduction

The third annual Old Vine Report sponsored by NFB Private Wealth Management is now out. There were 77 entries received from 48 producers and these were tasted blind (labels out of sight) by a three-person panel, scoring done according to the 100-point quality scale – 69% rated 90 or above.

Top 10

The 10 best wines overall are as follows:

96

FRAM Stagmanskop Chenin Blanc 2025
Price: R309
Wine of Origin: Piekenierskloof
Abv: 13.78%

Price: R269

Abv: 14%

Price: R285

Abv: 13%

Price: R650

Abv: 13.5%

Price: R185
Wine of Origin: Stellenbosch
Abv: 13%

 

Shop online

Online wine shop Getwine is offering all of the top wines for sale – buy wine.

About the category

The condition of entry for the Old Vine Report was that wines had to be made from Certified Heritage Vineyards (vines that are 35 years and older vines registered with SAWIS and approved by the Old Vine Project).

The South African old vines category continues to capture the attention of the international wine community, and the Old Vine Project has played a key role in this regard.  Founded as a non-profit company in 2016, it exists to promote the category among producers, trade, media and consumers.

The total area of old vines registered by SAWIS stood at 5,417ha in 2024, the equivalent of 6.3% of South Africa’s plantings.

What does top wine from old vines go for?

The average price of the 53 wines to rate 90-plus is R345 a bottle and of the Top 10 is R339.

In-depth analysis

To read the report in full, including key findings, tasting notes for the top wines, and buyers guide (wines ranked by quality relative to price), download the following: NFB Old Vine Report 2026

title: Clash of the titans: Bordeaux 2016 vs South Africa 2017
summary:
A wine can look very good in isolation. Put it alongside its counterparts from the rest of the world, and the context changes. In a tasting billed as “Clash of the Titans”, merchant Brice & Burnett pitted Bordeaux 2016 against South Africa 2017, two much celebrated vintages. The results were instructive, if not entirely comfortable […]

The post Clash of the titans: Bordeaux 2016 vs South Africa 2017 appeared first on winemag.
content:
A wine can look very good in isolation. Put it alongside its counterparts from the rest of the world, and the context changes. In a tasting billed as “Clash of the Titans”, merchant Brice & Burnett pitted Bordeaux 2016 against South Africa 2017, two much celebrated vintages. The results were instructive, if not entirely comfortable for local patriots.

The wines were tasted blind, one flight of three and three flights of four (B&B current prices in brackets).

Flight One
Du Terte Margaux 2016 – R1,250
Meerlust Rubicon 2017 – R750
Cantemerle Haut-Medoc 2016 – R975

Flight Two
Delaire Graff Botmaskop 2017 – R625
Keet First Verse 2017 – R1,025
Lafon-Rochet Saint-Estèphe 2016 – R1,450
Ernie Els Signature 2017 – R1,000

Flight Three
Kanonkop Paul Sauer 2017 – R1,425
Canon Saint-Emilion 2016 – R3,500
Domaine de Chevalier Pessac-Léognan Rouge 2016 – R2,300
Glenelly Lady May 2017 – N/A

Flight Four
Mvemve Raats De Compostella 2017 – N/A
Le Riche Cabernet Sauvignon Reserve 2017 – R1,295
Pichon-Longueville Baron Pauillac 2016 – R5,350
Lynch-Bages Pauillac 2016 – R4,950

Here’s how I rated the wines:

97
Lynch-Bages 2016

96
Canon 2016
Le Riche Cabenet Sauvignon Reserve 2017

95
Domaine de Chevalier Rouge 2016
Lafon-Rochet 2016
Mvemve Raats De Compostella

94
Delaire Graff Botmaskop 2017
Ernie Els Signature 2017

93
Glenelly Lady May 2017
Pichon-Longueville Baron 2016

92
Meerlust Rubicon 2017

91
Cantemerle 2016
Keet First Verse 2017

90
Du Tertre 2016

89
Kanonkop Paul Sauer 2017

Price, quality and the question of origin

The first point to make is that price and quality did not correlate particularly well. Lynch-Bages 2016, at R4,950, was my top wine at 97, but the R3,500 Canon 2016 managed 96, as did Le Riche Cabernet Sauvignon Reserve 2017 at R1,295. Mvemve Raats De Compostella 2017, current price unavailable although originally released at R1,500, also scored 95. These results suggest that serious quality is not the exclusive preserve of Bordeaux’s most expensive labels. Indeed, Le Riche offered a particularly compelling case for South African value. That said, a single tasting cannot establish a general relationship between price and quality, and the absence of retail prices for two local wines limits the comparison.

How did South Africa fare overall? Respectably, but with qualifications. Of the 15 wines, six South African examples scored 94 or above, against four Bordeaux wines. Yet Bordeaux claimed the top two scores, with Lynch-Bages at 97 and Canon at 96, while Kanonkop Paul Sauer 2017 brought up the rear at 89 (more on this below). The comparison is not quite as simple as the numbers suggest: the flights were small, and individual bottles, tasting order and stylistic preference inevitably influence results. Still, the strongest South African wines demonstrated that the country can compete at this level, even if the very top end of Bordeaux retained an edge.

I could identify the country of origin in 10 of the 15 instances. The Stellenbosch wines generally showed greater ripeness and higher alcohol, while retaining a degree of pyrazine character. This combination is revealing: Cabernet-based wines can be simultaneously generous and green, and ripeness alone does not guarantee completeness.

One further consideration is how much the wines had evolved. At roughly nine to ten years old, these were not merely exercises in youthful fruit and tannin. Scores were heavily influenced by the degree to which each wine had developed, and whether that development was positive. A wine that has shed its primary fruit without gaining complexity (Pichon Baron) is not necessarily better for the experience. Conversely, a wine retaining freshness, structure and interest (Lynch-Bages) after a decade deserves considerable credit.

Endurance is praiseworthy. The point of fine wine is not simply to impress when young, but to reward patience. On that measure, the most successful wines were those that are travelling well, not merely those that had started with the greatest reputation.

South Africa’s showing, wine by wine

A few brief remarks on each of the South African wines. Meerlust Rubicon 2017 was in good nick, if a relatively modest rendition of this famous wine. Delaire Graff Botmaskop and Ernie Els Signature both showed the precision and polish one would expect from these properties. Keet First Verse, at 15% alcohol, was relatively sweet and lacked structure, shortcomings I flagged on release (review here). Glenelly Lady May 2017 seems to be going through an awkward phase, its richness and firmness not yet reconciled and my sense is it’s nowhere near its peak. Mvemve Raats De Compostella was its usual elegant self, while Le Riche Cabernet Sauvignon Reserve displayed impressive structure and balance.

As for the Paul Sauer, perhaps we secretly like it for its oddness. It’s never been the most polished or immediately charming of wines, and its old-school, dikvoet character is part of its identity. But in this instance, those qualities seemed exaggerated, the wine showing as oxidised and raisined, with a kirsch-like quality to the fruit. Broad, flat and soft, it seemed to have little life left in it. This was not simply my own reaction; other tasters expressed similar reservations. One bottle is not a verdict on a wine, still less on a vintage. The 2017 could yet emerge gloriously with further bottle age, but this was a perplexing showing.

content:
Taste of Cape Town takes place at Green Point Cricket Club on 28 and 29 November, with 12 restaurants including La Colombe, FYN, Vuur, Upper Union, EDGE Africa and Basson & Co.

The festival will also feature live cooking demonstrations, music and wines from Boekenhoutskloof, Cavalli, Graham Beck, Kleine Zalze, Steenberg and Waterford. The City of Cape Town is a partner.

Tickets start at R450, with higher-priced options offering additional food and drinks. Capacity is limited to 4,000 people per day.

Tickets are available via Taste of Cape Town and Quicket.

Taste of Cape Town is organised by Johannesburg-based Allure Group, which holds the exclusive South African licence for the festival brand from international events company IMG.

content:
Introducing The Cold Soak, a podcast where we take a look at what’s been happening in South African wine – new releases, industry chatter, bold moves and questionable decisions.

Hosted by Ex Animo Wine Co.’s David Clarke and Winemag.co.za editor Christian Eedes, it brings together two informed, independent voices with a clear sense of perspective.

Episodes appear as regularly as possible, broadly following the rhythm of the wine month rather than a rigid schedule. Each one cuts through the noise with key releases, sharp takes on Winemag reports and candid discussion about where the industry is headed.

The approach is rigorous but unpretentious, analytical with a touch of humour – equally relevant to industry insiders and engaged drinkers alike.

Cape Winemakers Guild chair JD Pretorius recently joined us to discuss membership, auction wines, selection criteria and the Protégé Programme.

Listen to the latest episode here.

title: Michael Fridjhon: Why is Burgundy 10 times more expensive than the Cape?
summary:
One of the abiding lessons from the famous Judgement of Paris tasting hosted 50 years ago by the late Steven Spurrier in Paris is the discrepancy between the price points of New World producers and those of their competitors in the Old World. “Unknown” (not just to the French but also to all international markets) […]

The post Michael Fridjhon: Why is Burgundy 10 times more expensive than the Cape? appeared first on winemag.
content:
One of the abiding lessons from the famous Judgement of Paris tasting hosted 50 years ago by the late Steven Spurrier in Paris is the discrepancy between the price points of New World producers and those of their competitors in the Old World. “Unknown” (not just to the French but also to all international markets) Californian wines, selling for a fraction of what people were paying of top French wines, outperformed many of the world’s best-known wines from legendary appellations. Amongst the vanquished were Chateaux Mouton Rothschild and Haut Brion and a Batard Montrachet from Ramonet. 

Very little has changed since then. Yes, a few “iconic” international wines (Grange, Opus One) have seen their prices increase to align with the middle to upper end of the market (mainly in the last two decades), likewise some “unobtainable” cult wines (Harlan and Screaming Eagle, for example). But the gap between the leading New World producers and their European counterparts has not narrowed since then. Rather, it has increased significantly over the last half century.

Quality isn’t the problem

There are no technical reasons for this pricing discrepancy. Jancis Robinson recently reported on a series of blind tastings hosted by Smith and Sheth (the new big name in Kiwi Chardonnay) of their top cuvées lined up against some Burgundy collectibles. The most expensive New Zealand wine sells for under £100. The most expensive French wine – Domaine Leflaive Montrachet 2023 – retails for over £1,100. The only wine she scored above 18/20 (it finished on 18.5/20) was the Smith and Sheth Les Graviers 2024. Almost all of the Burgundies – and certainly all of the premiers and grands crus – price well into £250+ territory. These are not small pricing differentials – you could be talking about the produce of two different planets.

Meantime a very interesting study, published originally in the International Journal of Wine Business Research, analysed production practices and business strategies between Burgundy, New Zealand and South Africa. “Beyond terroir: a comparative analysis of Pinot Noir producers and business strategies in Burgundy, New Zealand and South Africa” (Depetris Chauvin, Pinède, & Priilaid, 2024) compared human capital, equipment and the working environment. The results were not necessarily surprising, though the extent of the differences is worth sharing: “92.9% of surveyed South African Pinot Noir wineries employ staff with formal oenology degrees (versus 39.5% in Burgundy), and 60.7% hold business degrees (versus 26.7% in Burgundy). • Technological Sophistication: South African producers post the highest winery equipment index across all three regions (60.1% vs. 49.6% in Burgundy), combining modern cellar automation with meticulous hand-harvesting (96.2%).”

There’s nothing surprising about either of these two outcomes – the Chardonnay tasting or the quantification of the technical competences of New World versus Old World producers. And this is actually where we should pause, and allow ourselves the surprise which would be the most likely reaction of a Martian presented with this evidence.

The price gap has widened

Fifty years after the Judgement of Paris tasting, half a century into an era in which it is widely recognised that fine wine does not have to come from a few appellations in France, the pricing differential in favour of the Old World has actually widened considerably. In the mid-1970s you could buy DRC Montrachet for R25-00, Jadot Montrachet for R15-00 and Chevalier Montrachet for R10-50. Krug cost R9-50 per bottle, Cristal R12-50, Chateau Leoville Lascases R10-50 and Chateau d’Yquem R25-00. At the same time Alto Cabernet sold for R3-50 and Theuniskraal Gewürztraminer (the highest priced SA white wine on the list I consulted) R1-90. These numbers tell us that R25-00 per bottle was the upper limit of price tolerance even for the world’s most iconic wines, and that South Africa’s most expensive cabernet sold for exactly one third the price of a Bordeaux Super Second.

Today – and if you exclude tiny volume wannabe cult wines whose pricing is not a reliable indicator of demand – this gap has widened. Currently Kanonkop Cabernet sells for one tenth the price of Leoville Lascases. The most expensive Cape chardonnays – say Delaire-Graff Terrace Block, Kershaw Deconstructed, or Capensis – hover around R1,500, which again is no more than 10% of the price of high-end (but not unobtainable) white Burgundy.

What happens next?

Two patterns are instantly discernible: the first is that the Old World has powered ahead price-wise despite the undisputed quality of the New World offering; the second is that the stratospheric pricing is simply a measure of demand from collectors and investors. This may have peaked, and could even be on the decline. There’s also no certainty, given climate change and the economics of fine wine, that the blue-chip purchases of 2026 will occupy the top slots on the ladder in 2076. But if prices really ease (and they should – much of what has fuelled their disproportionate increases has been worldwide demand for limited resource commodities) it’s also not certain that the New World will usurp these elevated price-points: if the bubble bursts it could lead to a complete realignment for everyone.

The past half century may have broadened the supplies of fine wine (and vastly increased the number of sites supplying them) but the primary beneficiaries have been the established producers of the Old World. This means that despite everything, the New World is still playing catch-up. Maybe with climate change (New Zealand’s chardonnays grow in a place which today is much cooler than the Cote de Beaune) the virtues of these more faraway appellations will become more evident. It’s possible that the Cape and the Antipodes will be the new centres of luxury wine in 2076, and the Old World’s best producers will be battling to make a living. What is clear however is that for now the pre-eminence of the Old World, as measured in retail price premium, remains unassailed.

  • Michael Fridjhon has over thirty-five years’ experience in the liquor industry. He is the founder of Winewizard.co.za and holds various positions including Visiting Professor of Wine Business at the University of Cape Town; founder and director of WineX – the largest consumer wine show in the Southern Hemisphere and chairman of The Trophy Wine Show.

title: Greg Sherwood MW: Can being an unknown wine region be an advantage?
summary:
If I mentioned the French wine region Duché d’Uzès (pronounce dooshay dooz) to any number of seasoned wine trade professionals globally, I am willing to wager a sizable sum that most, if not all, would never have heard of the appellation, and all would certainly have absolutely no idea where it lay on a map […]

The post Greg Sherwood MW: Can being an unknown wine region be an advantage? appeared first on winemag.
content:
If I mentioned the French wine region Duché d’Uzès (pronounce dooshay dooz) to any number of seasoned wine trade professionals globally, I am willing to wager a sizable sum that most, if not all, would never have heard of the appellation, and all would certainly have absolutely no idea where it lay on a map of France.

So, when I was invited on a press trip to this unknown appellation, I went straight to my bookshelf and pulled a copy of the Oxford Companion to Wine to explore further. As it turns out, it lies close to several not so obscure wine regions of France, including the wider Rhône Valley and the Languedoc.

Quietly tucked away into the northern reaches of the Gard department, between Nîmes, Avignon and the Cévennes foothills, the Duché d’Uzès appellation is one of France’s quieter wine secrets. Indeed, so quiet that in all my years of travelling in the Southern Rhône and the Languedoc Roussillon on buying trips, I had never once come across this little wine region over the past 30 years!

The region takes its name from Uzès, a honey-stoned market town village that interestingly held the title of France’s first duchy, created in 1565. Its ducal family still lives in the château that dominates the centre of the old town, and when we visited Uzès, the flag of the current fifty-something year old duke was flying above the castle indicating that he was in residence.

Few wine drinkers outside the region have heard of it probably because the appellation was only granted AOC (now called AOP or appellation d’origin protégé) status as recently as 2013, and it remains a tiny wine hamlet beside its more famous neighbours.

To the east, the famous Rhône Valley commands international attention with the famous names of Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Vacqueras, Gigondas and Rasteau. To the south and west, the broader Languedoc region dominates most wine conversations about value and innovation. Duché d’Uzès sits between them, often overlooked by visitors who come to visit the nearby Pont du Gard aqueduct or the lavender-scented lanes of nearby Provence.

It seems that obscurity is part of its appeal. Production is still small, with only 285 recognized AOP designated hectares of vines scattered across roughly twenty villages, with most bottles never leaving France. The terroir is fabulously distinctive: limestone and clay soils, garrigue scrubland, and vineyards planted at moderate altitudes, where cooler nights and the drying Mistral winds preserve freshness in the grapes.

The wines reflect their Rhône and Mediterranean heritage, reds built around Syrah, Grenache, Carignan, Cinsault and Mourvèdre, offering spice, dark fruits and a herbal, sun-warmed character. Whites, made from grapes such as Viognier, Grenache Blanc, Roussanne, Marsanne and Vermentino (Rolle), are aromatic and textured, with a saline lift. Dry Rosés round out most producers’ ranges, made from mostly 50/50 Grenache and Syrah grapes.

Many estates are family-run, often farming organically. For curious travelers and adventurous wine drinkers, Duché d’Uzès seems to offer something increasingly rare nowadays, namely authentic, characterful wines at modest prices, from a corner of Southern France still waiting to be discovered by the mainstream wine trade.

During my many numerous tastings with local Duché d’Uzès producers, I couldn’t help but compare their appellation’s obscurity with the relative hometown anonymity of Western Cape wine regions and wards such as Koekenaap, Slanghoek, Malgas, Bot Rivier, Baardskeerderbos and Piketberg. Similarly, fairly illustrious wine regions in the Cape producing some deliciously innovative wine styles. Nevertheless, most knowledgeable wine trade professionals across the UK, Europe or the USA would draw a blank if asked to recognise and pinpoint most of these wine localities.

Over dinner on one of the tasting evenings, it prompted a question from a Duché d’Uzès producer as to how I thought they should go about marketing their region to consumers in the UK? Or was that simply a very expensive marketing battle that was not worth fighting?

Somewhat paradoxically, I pointed out that in many ways, promoting a completely obscure region like Duché d’Uzès might in fact be an easier proposition than trying to convince young Gen Z’ers to drink Bordeaux. For many of them, these are the wines of their parents or grandparents and represent an abstract and somewhat old fashioned wine category that they would sooner avoid… that’s even presuming they could afford to buy the wines in the first place.

Unknown can mean novelty. Obscurity can equal a cool new wine discovery. After all, we are not talking about wines made from strange esoteric cultivars like those offered from Georgia, Turkey or Croatia. We are firmly in the realms of easily identifiable premium varietals such as Syrah, Grenache, Viognier and Cinsault.

With only circa 10% of the Duché d’Uzès wines exported, opening up new markets might seem like a lot of unnecessarily hard and expensive work when most of the wines can be sold locally cellar door or further afield around France. But home market sales are always vulnerable and with falling French consumption, especially for red wines, it’s always good to have a Plan B.

With many Duché d’Uzès producers pivoting towards dry white wines and Rosé styles, it makes sense to try and promote their succulent sun-kissed reds to a wider European audience. Similarly, the idea that South Africa’s local hotshot winemakers should take the easy path of least resistance and only sell their more obscure regional wines locally at home makes absolutely no commercial sense either.

The unknown should be embraced as just like the producers of Duché d’Uzès, South Africa’s producers making wines in more obscure regions, are for the most part, utilising grape cultivars that already have valuable international recognition and a ready appeal. This is an undeniable stoke of fortune that should not be overlooked or dismissed.

  • Greg Sherwood was born in Pretoria, South Africa, and as the son of a career diplomat, spent his first 21 years traveling the globe with his parents. With a Business Management and Marketing degree from Webster University, St. Louis, Missouri, USA, Sherwood began his working career as a commodity trader. In 2000, he decided to make more of a long-held interest in wine taking a position at Handford Wines in South Kensington, London, working his way up to the position of Senior Wine Buyer over 22 years. Sherwood currently consults to a number of top fine wine merchants in London while always keeping one eye firmly on the South African wine industry. He qualified as the 303rd Master of Wine in 2007.

The third annual Old Vine Report sponsored by NFB Private Wealth Management is now out. There were 77 entries received from 48 producers and these were tasted blind (labels out of sight) by a three-person panel, scoring done according to the 100-point quality scale – 69% rated 90 or above.

Shop online

Online wine shop Getwine is offering all of the top wines for sale – buy wine.

About the category

The condition of entry for the Old Vine Report was that wines had to be made from Certified Heritage Vineyards (vines that are 35 years and older vines registered with SAWIS and approved by the Old Vine Project).

The South African old vines category continues to capture the attention of the international wine community, and the Old Vine Project has played a key role in this regard.  Founded as a non-profit company in 2016, it exists to promote the category among producers, trade, media and consumers.

The total area of old vines registered by SAWIS stood at 5,417ha in 2024, the equivalent of 6.3% of South Africa’s plantings.

What does top wine from old vines go for?

The average price of the 53 wines to rate 90-plus is R345 a bottle and of the Top 10 is R339.

In-depth analysis

To read the report in full, including key findings, tasting notes for the top wines, and buyers guide (wines ranked by quality relative to price), download the following: NFB Old Vine Report 2026

The post Clash of the titans: Bordeaux 2016 vs South Africa 2017 appeared first on winemag.
content:
A wine can look very good in isolation. Put it alongside its counterparts from the rest of the world, and the context changes. In a tasting billed as “Clash of the Titans”, merchant Brice & Burnett pitted Bordeaux 2016 against South Africa 2017, two much celebrated vintages. The results were instructive, if not entirely comfortable for local patriots.

The wines were tasted blind, one flight of three and three flights of four (B&B current prices in brackets).

Flight One
Du Terte Margaux 2016 – R1,250
Meerlust Rubicon 2017 – R750
Cantemerle Haut-Medoc 2016 – R975

Flight Two
Delaire Graff Botmaskop 2017 – R625
Keet First Verse 2017 – R1,025
Lafon-Rochet Saint-Estèphe 2016 – R1,450
Ernie Els Signature 2017 – R1,000

Flight Three
Kanonkop Paul Sauer 2017 – R1,425
Canon Saint-Emilion 2016 – R3,500
Domaine de Chevalier Pessac-Léognan Rouge 2016 – R2,300
Glenelly Lady May 2017 – N/A

Flight Four
Mvemve Raats De Compostella 2017 – N/A
Le Riche Cabernet Sauvignon Reserve 2017 – R1,295
Pichon-Longueville Baron Pauillac 2016 – R5,350
Lynch-Bages Pauillac 2016 – R4,950

Here’s how I rated the wines:

97
Lynch-Bages 2016

96
Canon 2016
Le Riche Cabenet Sauvignon Reserve 2017

95
Domaine de Chevalier Rouge 2016
Lafon-Rochet 2016
Mvemve Raats De Compostella

94
Delaire Graff Botmaskop 2017
Ernie Els Signature 2017

93
Glenelly Lady May 2017
Pichon-Longueville Baron 2016

92
Meerlust Rubicon 2017

91
Cantemerle 2016
Keet First Verse 2017

90
Du Tertre 2016

89
Kanonkop Paul Sauer 2017

Price, quality and the question of origin

The first point to make is that price and quality did not correlate particularly well. Lynch-Bages 2016, at R4,950, was my top wine at 97, but the R3,500 Canon 2016 managed 96, as did Le Riche Cabernet Sauvignon Reserve 2017 at R1,295. Mvemve Raats De Compostella 2017, current price unavailable although originally released at R1,500, also scored 95. These results suggest that serious quality is not the exclusive preserve of Bordeaux’s most expensive labels. Indeed, Le Riche offered a particularly compelling case for South African value. That said, a single tasting cannot establish a general relationship between price and quality, and the absence of retail prices for two local wines limits the comparison.

How did South Africa fare overall? Respectably, but with qualifications. Of the 15 wines, six South African examples scored 94 or above, against four Bordeaux wines. Yet Bordeaux claimed the top two scores, with Lynch-Bages at 97 and Canon at 96, while Kanonkop Paul Sauer 2017 brought up the rear at 89 (more on this below). The comparison is not quite as simple as the numbers suggest: the flights were small, and individual bottles, tasting order and stylistic preference inevitably influence results. Still, the strongest South African wines demonstrated that the country can compete at this level, even if the very top end of Bordeaux retained an edge.

I could identify the country of origin in 10 of the 15 instances. The Stellenbosch wines generally showed greater ripeness and higher alcohol, while retaining a degree of pyrazine character. This combination is revealing: Cabernet-based wines can be simultaneously generous and green, and ripeness alone does not guarantee completeness.

One further consideration is how much the wines had evolved. At roughly nine to ten years old, these were not merely exercises in youthful fruit and tannin. Scores were heavily influenced by the degree to which each wine had developed, and whether that development was positive. A wine that has shed its primary fruit without gaining complexity (Pichon Baron) is not necessarily better for the experience. Conversely, a wine retaining freshness, structure and interest (Lynch-Bages) after a decade deserves considerable credit.

Endurance is praiseworthy. The point of fine wine is not simply to impress when young, but to reward patience. On that measure, the most successful wines were those that are travelling well, not merely those that had started with the greatest reputation.

South Africa’s showing, wine by wine

A few brief remarks on each of the South African wines. Meerlust Rubicon 2017 was in good nick, if a relatively modest rendition of this famous wine. Delaire Graff Botmaskop and Ernie Els Signature both showed the precision and polish one would expect from these properties. Keet First Verse, at 15% alcohol, was relatively sweet and lacked structure, shortcomings I flagged on release (review here). Glenelly Lady May 2017 seems to be going through an awkward phase, its richness and firmness not yet reconciled and my sense is it’s nowhere near its peak. Mvemve Raats De Compostella was its usual elegant self, while Le Riche Cabernet Sauvignon Reserve displayed impressive structure and balance.

As for the Paul Sauer, perhaps we secretly like it for its oddness. It’s never been the most polished or immediately charming of wines, and its old-school, dikvoet character is part of its identity. But in this instance, those qualities seemed exaggerated, the wine showing as oxidised and raisined, with a kirsch-like quality to the fruit. Broad, flat and soft, it seemed to have little life left in it. This was not simply my own reaction; other tasters expressed similar reservations. One bottle is not a verdict on a wine, still less on a vintage. The 2017 could yet emerge gloriously with further bottle age, but this was a perplexing showing.
